title: Understand that a function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output

steps.text: I can tell that a function gives each input exactly one output.
steps.example: Each student → one birth month, so it is a function.

steps.text: I can use the vertical line test to tell if a graph is a function.
steps.example: A circle is not a function: a vertical line hits it twice.

steps.text: I can tell if a table or list of points is a function.
steps.example: (2, 5) and (2, 7): not a function, 2 has two outputs.

steps.text: I can find the domain (inputs) and range (outputs) of a function.
I can find f(x) when I know x.
I can find the input that gives a certain output.
I can use a table or graph to find where a function changes fastest.
steps.example: Tank drops 2 gal/min from 0–8 min, 12.5 gal/min from 8–10 → fastest 8–10.

steps.text: I can explain why a relation is or is not a function.
steps.example: x = y² fails: input 4 has two outputs, 2 and −2.

steps.text: I can give a domain and range that make sense in a real situation.
steps.example: Buy 0 to 6 tickets at $9: domain {0, 1, …, 6}, range {0, 9, …, 54}

title: Identify linear and nonlinear functions; interpret y = mx + b

steps.text: I can tell if a table, graph, or equation is linear or nonlinear.
steps.example: y = x² + 1 is nonlinear: its graph curves.

steps.text: I can name a slope as positive, negative, zero, or undefined.
steps.example: Flat (horizontal) line: zero slope. Vertical line: undefined.

steps.text: I can find the slope m and the y-intercept b in y = mx + b.
I can find the slope of a line on a graph using rise over run.
steps.example: Up 8, right 2 → slope = 8 ÷ 2 = 4

steps.text: I can tell how a line changes when m or b changes.
steps.example: y = 2x + 1 → y = 5x − 3: steeper, crosses 4 lower

steps.text: I can write y = mx + b from a graph or a table.
I can write y = mx + b when the table skips x = 0.
I can explain why y = mx + b always changes by the same amount.
steps.example: y = 4x + 3: each time x goes up 1, y goes up 4.

title: Construct a function to model a linear relationship

steps.text: I can tell if a real situation changes by the same amount each time.
steps.example: Taxi: $3 plus $2 per mile is linear.

steps.text: I can find the rate of change and starting value in a table or story.
steps.example: $45, $57, $69 each week → $12 per week, start $45

steps.text: I can write y = mx + b from a story.
steps.example: Starts at 80 ft, drops 4 ft each second → y = −4x + 80

steps.text: I can use the slope formula to find slope from two points.
I can write y = mx + b from two points.
I can build a model from two facts in a story and use it.
steps.example: 2 h costs $170, 5 h costs $335 → y = 55x + 60

steps.text: I can build a model with decimals from real data and use units.
I can explain why a situation is linear or not linear.
steps.example: +$10 each week is linear; doubling each week is not.

title: Compare properties of two functions represented in different ways

steps.text: I can find the slope and start value in a table, graph, or equation.
steps.example: x: 0, 1, 2 and y: 7, 9, 11 → slope 2, start 7

steps.text: I can tell what the slope and y-intercept mean in a story.
steps.example: Taxi y = 2.50x + 4: $4 is paid before any miles.

steps.text: I can tell which of two functions grows faster and which starts higher.
steps.example: y = 3x + 1 grows faster; y = 2x + 7 starts higher.

steps.text: I can put functions in order by slope when they are shown in different ways.
steps.example: Graph slope 4, table slope 3, y = −2x + 10 → 4, 3, −2

steps.text: I can use a linear function to make a prediction.
steps.example: Battery y = −0.6x + 100 → 40% left after 100 minutes

steps.text: I can find when two functions have the same output.
steps.example: 3x + 2 = 4x − 3 → same output at x = 5

steps.text: I can compare two functions to decide what happens and explain with numbers.
steps.example: Mia d = 5t + 30, Jon d = 7t: Jon reaches 200 m first.

steps.text: I can tell which points make sense in the story and which do not.
steps.example: Gift card y = −15x + 240: (20, −60) makes no sense.

title: Describe and sketch graphs that show how two quantities are related
student_title: Tell the story of a graph

steps.text: I can tell where a graph goes up, goes down, or stays flat.
steps.example: Graph falls from 25 to 40 seconds → decreasing.

steps.text: I can tell if part of a graph is linear (straight) or nonlinear (curved).
steps.example: A straight piece is linear; a curved piece is nonlinear.

steps.text: I can match a story to its graph.
steps.example: Fill tub, take bath, drain → up, flat, down to 0.

steps.text: I can describe each part of a graph with its start and end times.
steps.example: Increasing 0 to 2 h, constant 2 to 3 h, decreasing 3 to 5 h

steps.text: I can sketch a graph from a story with several parts.
steps.example: Kite rises 2 min, then stays 3 min → slant up, then flat.

steps.text: I can use the rate of change to explain if a part is linear.
steps.example: Up 10, then 20, then 30 m each minute → nonlinear.

steps.text: I can explain what each part of a graph means in the story.
steps.example: Gas graph: down = driving, flat = parked, jump up = filled up.

steps.text: I can sketch a curved graph and explain why it curves.
steps.example: Ball falls 5, 15, 25 m each second: faster, so it curves.

title: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate data

steps.text: I can make a scatter plot from a table of data.
steps.example: Week 1, 30 words per minute → plot (1, 30).

steps.text: I can tell if an association is positive, negative, or none.
steps.example: Hotter days, less hot cocoa sold → negative

steps.text: I can tell if an association is linear or nonlinear.
steps.example: Bacteria double every hour → points curve, so nonlinear.

steps.text: I can find clusters and outliers in a scatter plot.
steps.example: Clusters at 4–6 h and 18–21 h; (20, 90) is an outlier.

steps.text: I can tell if an association is strong or weak.
steps.example: Points stay close to an upward line → strong positive

steps.text: I can compare the associations in two scatter plots.
steps.example: Lemonade: strong positive. Soup: weak negative.

steps.text: I can describe a whole scatter plot and say what it means.
steps.example: More screen time, less sleep: negative, two clusters, one outlier.

steps.text: I can predict if a real situation is linear and explain why.
steps.example: Height from age 0 to 30 is not linear: growth slows, then stops.

title: Informally fit a straight line to a scatter plot
student_title: Draw a line of best fit

steps.text: I can explain that a line of best fit shows the trend, not every point.
steps.example: A good line can miss most points, with some above and below.

steps.text: I can draw a line of best fit through the middle of the points.
steps.example: About half the points above the line, half below.

steps.text: I can tell if a line fits well by how close the points are.
steps.example: Points close on both sides → good fit; all points above → poor fit.

steps.text: I can find the slope of a line of best fit from two points on it.
I can write the equation of a line of best fit.
I can explain how an outlier can pull a line of best fit away.
steps.example: One very high point pulled the line's right end up.

steps.text: I can choose the better of two lines and prove it with distances.
steps.example: Line A: all points within 1. Line B: some 4 off → A.

steps.text: I can tell how much to trust a line's predictions by how close the points are.
steps.example: Points far from the line → weak model, so predictions are rough.

title: Use a linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate data

steps.text: I can explain what the slope means in a data model.
steps.example: y = −8x + 100: battery drops 8% each hour.

steps.text: I can explain what the y-intercept means in a data model.
steps.example: y = 15x + 40: Malik started with $40.

steps.text: I can put in an x-value to make a prediction.
I can solve for x when I know the y-value.
I can write a model from a story and use it to answer a question.
steps.example: $25 fee + $30 a month: 30x + 25 = 295 → 9 months

steps.text: I can use one point on a model to find a missing slope.
steps.example: y = mx + 15 through (4, 75) → m = 15

steps.text: I can write a model from two data points and make a prediction.
I can decide if a prediction makes sense or goes too far.
steps.example: Height y = 2.5x + 29: age 30 → 104 in., not reasonable.

title: Construct and interpret two-way tables for categorical data

steps.text: I can read a count and a total from a two-way table.
steps.example: 7th grade row, Skip column: 25 students skip breakfast.

steps.text: I can fill in a two-way table with totals from a story.
steps.example: 50 seventh graders, 30 like paper → 20 like screens.

steps.text: I can find a relative frequency: count ÷ total.
steps.example: 48 of 125 bought candy: 48 ÷ 125 = 38.4%

steps.text: I can find a percent for just one row or column.
steps.example: 12 of 80 students who live far bike: 12 ÷ 80 = 15%

steps.text: I can explain what a relative frequency means in the story.
steps.example: 18 ÷ 60 = 0.3: 30% of shoppers under 25 paid cash.

steps.text: I can explain why I compare percents, not just counts.
steps.example: 30 of 60 is 50%, but 30 of 100 is only 30%.

steps.text: I can compare percents to decide if there is an association.
steps.example: Curfew: 70% get 8+ hours; no curfew: 40% → association

steps.text: I can explain what it means when there is no association.
steps.example: 62.5% of lefties and righties like dogs → no association.
